title: The Department of Neuromodulation
subtitle: A "The Frontier Psychiatrists" Beijing Dispatch
body_html:
“All hospitals look the same,” I found myself saying out loud as the myriad faculty at the Beijing Anding Hospital led me down the hall from their current offices to their “new digs,” one building over.

The halls were a shade of off-white that Gods, the world over, have reserved for medical facilities. The floors were smart tile: tidy and well laid. The bathrooms were different than I expected. There were green plants growing, with leafy vines snaking above urinals. They had the kind of low-key “greenwall energy” that makes Brooklyn eateries such a breath of fresh air.

Its leader is the laconic but very funny physician, Gang Wang (in Mandarin, 王刚). He’s about my height, if in better shape, with close-cropped hair, thin-rimmed glasses, and a quick smile. Dr. Wang is responsible for managing care at the scale of 1.2 million outpatient visits a year. He was also the phase III principal investigator for what would be branded Cobenfy in China. Imagine Shakespeare’s Puck ended up as a senior administrator at mind-bending scale, leading AI model development efforts, and you will be on the right track.

China has on the order of 38,000 hospitals nationwide. Similar to the US, it’s a three-tier system, with the tertiary centers of expertise the equivalent of our “level-one” trauma centers at premier academic institutions. Similar to the US (in the 1800s), free-standing psychiatric hospitals exist, and are the mainstay of psychiatric care in mainland China. China has 2,277 specialized psychiatric hospitals nationwide, and about 56,000 psychiatrists. The total number of psychiatric beds is 840,871. These numbers have been going up substantially since 2019.

Psychiatrists are seeing on the order of 30-50 patients a day. Virtually all doctors work for a hospital, which offers both inpatient and outpatient visits. There are also private clinics, open evenings and weekends, in which one can pay 10× the reimbursement from government insurance to be seen for longer, without the wait.

China has state insurance, like most of the rest of the world. State insurance in China all has what we’d call “coinsurance,” and this amount varies across types of care. Many services will be covered at 70% of the cost, some less. Some medicines are only available privately—Spravato, for example, is only covered for it’s MDSI indication, so patients need to be suicidal. There is, after all, only one formulary.

Beijing Anding Hospital, associated with Capital Medical University, has an entire Department of Neuromodulation.

Their transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) clinic is sprawling, with the main TMS treatment room offering treatment to around 15 patients at once with an array of figure-of-eight devices. TMS treatment is between $8-$21 per stimulation in public clinics, or 10× that in private clinics, equal to US rates.

Other rooms in the department held investigational devices, regulated under the same Good Clinical Practice (GCP) standards I have to uphold at home in NYC. These include studies using novel approaches such as tDCS, temporal interference, transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS), and more.

Honestly, walking through this hospital’s Department of Neuromodulation, I felt seen. Here is an entire department of a hospital that spends all day thinking about the same things that I do. They’re treating about 150,000 patients a year with transcranial magnetic stimulation at just this one center. Because the cost is relatively low, the doctors are not restricted in what they can treat with TMS. If they read a paper, and there’s evidence to treat auditory hallucinations, or OCD, or anxiety, or insomnia, they can treat it. Thus, more data gets generated. More papers get published. More healing happens. It’s all about the price point at which authorities, no matter where they are, start worrying about how much money they’re spending. Transcranial magnetic stimulation, and neuromodulation generally, is a little bit like a genie. It can grant many wishes, but people get nervous about that possibility, if they don’t like letting genies out of bottles. China solves that problem by keeping the cost low.

One thing that is similar about the Chinese and American systems of payment is that neither system has figured out how to pay for accelerated transcranial magnetic stimulation yet.

Here I was watching targeting become unrestrained, with access to functional magnetic resonance imaging, EEG, and other biomarkers, but the administrative task of figuring out how to submit more than one treatment in a day and have systems process that payment just hasn’t been worked out.

I’m glad the madness that is the system of healthcare payment is not exclusive to my experience!

The doctors I met were more up-to-date than most of my US colleagues, and doing more audacious research than I’m used to seeing anywhere outside of a brain stimulation annual meeting. Unlike most of my brain stimulation colleagues, my Chinese colleagues were already “all in” on the AI diagnostic approaches that I have been advocating for many years. I watched lectures, during the CNS Summit co-sponsored meeting, on using extraocular gaze tracking, EEG, fMRI, Circular RNA, and other advanced technology to understand what the treatment should be for each individual patient.

As the author of myriad papers on both neuromodulation and AI-guided diagnostics, it felt like coming home, intellectually. I felt less alone, and like there might be tremendous hope for the patients I care so much about. Scientists and healers are dedicating their lives to answering the same questions that make me seem like a starry-eyed dreamer “back home.”
